section_summary: This section documents U.S. official and public concern over exports of strategic materials to Japan, including petroleum, copper, cobalt, zinc, scrap iron and steel, mercury, fluorspar, fusel oil, storage tanks, and industrial equipment. State Department memoranda assess Japanese stockpiling, possible re-export to Germany, weaknesses in existing export controls, and shipments from Latin America and the Philippines, while replies to citizens and legislators explain or defend current licensing policy. The section also contains advocacy correspondence supporting stronger economic pressure on Japan and aid to China, together with reports from Tokyo, London, Madrid, Mexico, Chile, and Peru.

subfiles.title: Continuation of memorandum on Japanese copper orders
subfiles.about: Compares copper quantities for 1938–1940 and warns that Japanese orders after the July embargoes indicate stockpiling.
subfiles.summary: Page of copper totals for 1938, 1939 and early 1940, noting about 150 million pounds ordered after July 1940, an excessive rate.

subfiles.title: Cobalt Shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports a large Belgian Congo cobalt cargo consigned to Mitsui and Mitsubishi and considers embargoing it.
subfiles.summary: The Westhumaw was to bring 426 tons of cobalt for Mitsui and 105 for Mitsubishi, about a year's Japanese supply, raising suspicion of onward shipment to Germany; Britain might otherwise halt Congo cobalt trade.

subfiles.title: Record of Mr. Stannard's call concerning Japanese copper buying in Chile
subfiles.about: Records a copper-company representative's warning that Japanese trading houses might request introductions for copper negotiations in Chile.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Stannard says Japanese trading houses like Mitsui invited him to lunch and he expects requests for introductions to Chilean copper officials.

subfiles.title: Canadian reports on scrap iron and zinc procurement in Colombia
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Forwards Canadian Legation memoranda concerning Japanese efforts to obtain scrap iron and zinc through Colombia.
subfiles.summary: Green encloses memoranda on Canadian Metals Controller Bateman's correspondence, an approach to Fujiye Trading about scrap iron, and Okura's report to Mitsui on Colombian zinc.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department referral of Mata B. Roudin letter
subfiles.from: James W. Young, Director, Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Refers Mata B. Roudin's letter about gasoline exports to the State Department for attention.
subfiles.summary: Commerce refers Mata Roudin's letter to Green's office; the writer was advised.

subfiles.title: Routing sheets for Mata B. Roudin correspondence
subfiles.about: Summarizes and routes Roudin's inquiry about large gasoline shipments to Japan under government permits.
subfiles.summary: The two substantially duplicate sheets identify a December 8 letter from Mata B. Roudin of New York City. They request a direct reply regarding reports that large quantities of gasoline were being shipped to Japan under special permits.

subfiles.title: Letter questioning gasoline shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Questions continued gasoline shipments to Japan despite the government's export policy.
subfiles.summary: The letter is severely degraded in the OCR, but its routing description identifies the subject as large gasoline shipments to Japan under special government permits. Roudin asks the Secretary of Commerce for an explanation.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mata B. Roudin on gasoline regulations
subfiles.from: Leonard H. Price, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that the July 1940 regulations prohibited only gasoline meeting the defined aviation-grade threshold.
subfiles.summary: Price says only aviation gasoline of ASTM octane rating 87 or more, including gasoline reaching that with limited tetraethyl lead, was prohibited under the July 26 regulations, and later shipments didn't meet it.

subfiles.title: Exports of crude oil and gasoline to Japan through December 1940
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Reports a December surge in gasoline exports to Japan and supplies monthly petroleum export figures.
subfiles.summary: Yost notes that gasoline exports rose sharply in December while crude-oil exports declined. Much of the gasoline was medium-grade aviation fuel that could be converted easily into higher-quality fuel. A table compares the first eight months of 1940 with September through December and also gives annual totals for 1939.

subfiles.title: Petroleum exports, outstanding licenses, and related equipment
subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese petroleum imports, outstanding export licenses, and possible controls on drums, tanks, and oil-field equipment.
subfiles.summary: Yost: nearly 3.5 million barrels of gasoline went to Japan in 1940 with about four million barrels still licensed, much usable in military aircraft; he discusses lowering the octane limit, restricting exports to prewar levels, and licensing drums and tanks.

subfiles.title: War Department transmittal of Dr. King's letter
subfiles.to: Cecil W. Gray, Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards George S. King's inquiry about exports to Japan for State Department action.
subfiles.summary: War Department forwards Dr. George King's letter to Stimson, since the issue belongs to State.

subfiles.title: Dr. King's protest against gasoline and armor-plate exports
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Protests alleged exports of gasoline and armor plate to Japan and suspected transshipment through Mexico.
subfiles.summary: King argues commercial gasoline could be converted to aviation fuel, questions reports Japan could buy armor plate and get scrap and oil via Mexico, and calls the policy irrational and dangerous.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to George S. King
subfiles.from: Leonard H. Price, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Assures King that export licenses are reviewed for national-defense concerns and denies the reported armor-plate and Mexican transshipment claims.
subfiles.summary: Price says no armor-plate license for Japan was issued that year and no reason exists to think scrap iron and oil sent to Mexico were unlawfully transshipped to Japan.

subfiles.title: Memorandum summarizing J. Leighton Stuart's circular
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Sumner Welles, and the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes Stuart's appeal for comprehensive economic pressure on Japan and his assessment of possible Japanese responses.
subfiles.summary: Summary of J. Leighton Stuart's circular: Americans in North China approve scrap restrictions and want wider measures; he foresees continued aggression, retrenchment or tactical concessions and urges holding firm.

subfiles.title: Roger S. Greene's forwarding letter for Stuart circular
subfiles.about: Forwards Leighton Stuart's October 19 circular and recommends that it be shown to Secretary Hull.
subfiles.summary: Greene asks Hornbeck to present Stuart's circular to Hull and praises his far-sighted attitude toward Yenching University's difficulties.

subfiles.title: Confidential circular to the Board of Trustees of Yenching University
subfiles.to: Board of Trustees of Yenching University
subfiles.about: Advocates sustained American economic pressure on Japan and describes the dangers facing Yenching University.
subfiles.summary: Stuart's circular to Yenching trustees endorses the steel and scrap ban and broader restrictions, warns of superficial Japanese concessions, and describes evacuation planning and staff determination to remain.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgment to Roger S. Greene
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Greene's letter and states that Stuart's circular is being circulated within the Department.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Greene for Stuart's confidential October 19 letter, noted with interest and passed to other officers.

subfiles.title: Illegible separator page
subfiles.about: Contains no recoverable substantive document text.
subfiles.summary: Only a short stray OCR fragment is visible on this page. No subject, author, recipient, or date can be identified.

subfiles.title: Orrin G. Judd letter on exports to Japan and Brooklyn meeting
subfiles.about: Urges expansion of the embargo and requests a State Department speaker for a Brooklyn meeting on China.
subfiles.summary: Orrin Judd says Brooklyn residents can't understand continued exports of copper, oil and machinery to Japan, asks Hull to press for wider restrictions, and invites a representative to a December 14 meeting.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Orrin G. Judd
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains current export controls and declines to send an officer to Judd's Brooklyn meeting.
subfiles.summary: Allen encloses the Export Control Act and notes scrap, aviation gasoline and lubricating oil are restricted to the Western Hemisphere and Britain; no officer can attend the December 14 luncheon.

subfiles.title: Brooklyn Committee letter demanding an explanation of Japan trade policy
subfiles.about: Asks why the United States continues supplying Japan and requests a speaker or policy statement for a Brooklyn conference.
subfiles.summary: Brooklyn Committee's Boulton welcomes the China loan and some license refusals but says the U.S. still supplies most of Japan's war materials; she requests a speaker or policy statement for a December 14 meeting.

subfiles.title: Says Japan Gets Zinc Needed Here
subfiles.from: Associated Press report quoting C. Donald Dallas
subfiles.about: Reports that zinc exports to Japan were causing shortages for American and British brass production.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: 3,775 tons of zinc went to Japan in October and 12,042 tons in ten months of 1940, while domestic brass plants curtailed defense production; it urges new supplies or diverting zinc from consumer uses.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Frances S. Boulton
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the export-control framework and declines to provide a Department speaker for the December 14 luncheon.
subfiles.summary: The damaged first page nevertheless parallels the Department's reply to Judd and encloses the Export Control Act and implementing measures. Allen says restrictions vary according to American defense needs and remain under continuing study. He declines the luncheon invitation because of the Department's heavy workload.

subfiles.title: Harry B. Price cover letter to Maxwell Hamilton
subfiles.about: Forwards a copy of Price's letter to Export Control Administrator Russell L. Maxwell.
subfiles.summary: Harry Price sends Hamilton a copy of his letter to Colonel Maxwell on the adequacy of export controls on materials going to Japan.

subfiles.title: Price letter criticizing limited export controls
subfiles.about: Urges wider licensing of war materials and questions Maxwell's apparent effort to minimize existing restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Price argues the Export Control Act allows withholding strategic materials from potential enemies and public opinion favors broader limits; citing zinc shortages, he asks whether Maxwell means to limit the controls' effect.

subfiles.title: Oil Export Control May Bar Only Plane Fuel
subfiles.from: New York Herald Tribune / Associated Press
subfiles.about: Reports Maxwell's effort to confine petroleum controls to aviation fuel and discusses possible licensing of zinc.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: Maxwell sought to limit oil export controls to aircraft fuel; zinc controls are studied after Dallas's warning, and zinc may soon need licenses.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for file 894.24/1205
subfiles.about: Records the temporary charging-out of document 894.24/1205.
subfiles.summary: Charge slip for file 894.24/1205 with date and clerk notation.

subfiles.title: Internal routing instructions concerning the Lazaron correspondence
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.to: Division of Controls and Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Directs preparation and routing of a reply concerning the Institute of Scrap Iron and Steel.
subfiles.summary: The fragmentary typed and handwritten notes ask the Division of Controls to draft a response. The proposed routing appears to call for the draft to pass through Far Eastern Affairs before returning to the senior official.

subfiles.title: Welles note requesting Hornbeck's advice
subfiles.about: Asks what reply should be made to Morris S. Lazaron.
subfiles.summary: Welles asks Hornbeck's advice on Lazaron's inquiry about the scrap-iron trade organization's invitation.

subfiles.title: Lazaron request for advice about scrap-industry banquet
subfiles.about: Requests counsel on whether to deliver the invocation at the Institute of Scrap Iron and Steel banquet.
subfiles.summary: Lazaron, invited to give the invocation at the scrap institute's January Baltimore convention, is inclined to refuse and asks Welles's advice.

subfiles.title: Welles reply regarding the Institute of Scrap Iron and Steel
subfiles.about: Advises Lazaron that the scrap-industry institute cooperated with the government and that he need not decline its invitation.
subfiles.summary: Welles says press portrayals of scrap dealers as obstinate were unfair, the institute helped before the ban, and Lazaron has no reason to refuse the invocation.
keywords: Institute of Scrap Iron and Steel

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Mr. Buffum on aviation gasoline policy
subfiles.about: Records Buffum's criticism of policy toward Japanese refinery plants and aviation-gasoline exports.
subfiles.summary: Buffum says Japan, allowed to buy refineries, spent its money stockpiling gasoline able to make 90-octane fuel; he suggests quietly changing test specifications to cut quality exportable under existing licenses.

subfiles.title: Senator Johnson's transmittal of Colorado organizations' telegram
subfiles.about: Forwards a protest concerning an alleged shipment of scrap-iron billets to Japan and requests a prompt report.
subfiles.summary: Senator Johnson forwards a Colorado Friends of the Chinese People telegram and asks State for prompt advice.

subfiles.title: Telegram alleging shipment of scrap billets to Japan
subfiles.from: Colorado Friends of the Chinese People and Denver Chapter, American Bureau for Medical Aid to China
subfiles.about: Alleges that 86 carloads of scrap iron were melted into billets to evade the export ban and loaded for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Telegram alleges Colorado Fuel and Iron's Minnequa Plant made scrap into billets to evade the ban, loaded December 20 on the Tosei Maru for Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Johnson on alleged billet shipment
subfiles.about: Reports that the alleged export-license application could not be identified and encloses the December 10 iron-and-steel regulations.
subfiles.summary: Hull says license applications couldn't identify the shipment from the details given, and encloses the President's December 10 proclamation and iron and steel regulations.

subfiles.title: Fusel oil uses and possible Japanese stockpiling
subfiles.from: Jones, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Explains fusel oil's industrial and military uses and recommends circulating the Tokyo report to relevant agencies.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum: fusel oil is mainly amyl alcohol; rising Japanese purchases suggest stockpiling or buying for Germany, the latter likelier; copies of the telegram are recommended for officials.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram on increased fusel-oil shipments
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports unusually large American fusel-oil shipments to Japan and continued Mitsui purchasing above market prices.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo telegram: other-alcohol exports including fusel oil reached 1,878,200 pounds in 11 months of 1940, against 928,700 in 1939; Mitsui keeps buying at twenty percent over market.

subfiles.title: Paraphrases of Tokyo fusel-oil telegram
subfiles.about: Provides two paraphrased copies of the Embassy's report on Japanese fusel-oil purchases.
subfiles.summary: The copies restate the Tokyo Embassy's warning that shipments of fusel oil from the United States to Japan had increased sharply. They reproduce the comparative figures for 1938–1940 and report that Mitsui continued purchasing at twenty percent above the prevailing market price.

subfiles.title: British Embassy report on oil-storage tanks exported to Japan
subfiles.about: Records a British Embassy statement about a large December shipment of petroleum-storage tanks to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck notes a January 6 discussion with Butler and Hill; tanks exported December 21, mostly 9,000-barrel units, could store about 1.1 million barrels of petroleum products.

subfiles.title: London telegram on British refusal of Japanese tank gear-box exports
subfiles.from: Herschel V. Johnson, American Embassy London
subfiles.about: Reports British controversy over and final refusal of an export license for gear-box parts intended for Japan.
subfiles.summary: London telegram: after worker protests, a prewar contract for gear boxes of a Japanese tank type was found; permission for remaining parts was refused, leaving about 17,500 pounds of goods useless.

subfiles.title: Antofagasta despatch on copper shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: George H. Adams, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Reports large January–February copper shipments from Antofagasta to Japan and encloses a detailed sailing schedule.
subfiles.summary: Antofagasta: Chile Exploration plans to ship 12,720 long tons of copper to Japan and 11,350 to the U.S.; sudden Japanese demand for semi-refined copper raised suspicion. Enclosure lists vessels and destinations.

subfiles.title: Voorhis inquiry about crude oil mixed with Ethyl
subfiles.about: Relays an allegation that Standard Oil in California was mixing crude oil with Ethyl and selling it to Japan as crude.
subfiles.summary: Voorhis, lacking proof, asks investigation of a report that equal parts crude oil and Ethyl were sold to Japan as crude oil.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Voorhis on crude-oil mixtures
subfiles.about: Explains licensing rules for crude oil mixed with tetraethyl lead, aviation lubricant, or Ethyl gasoline.
subfiles.summary: Hull says no licenses covered tetraethyl lead, aviation lubricating oil or aviation gasoline for Japan; crude mixed with such products wouldn't be released without licenses, and Ethyl gasoline only below the octane threshold.

subfiles.title: Madrid telegram on Japanese purchase of Spanish mercury
subfiles.from: Alexander W. Weddell, American Embassy Madrid
subfiles.about: Reports Mitsubishi's purchase of 253 flasks of mercury from the Spanish Almadén mines.
subfiles.summary: Madrid telegram: Almaden mines sold Mitsubishi 253 more flasks of mercury, valued at 63,250, to go from Vigo to Yokohama via New York aboard the Artigas.

subfiles.title: Exportation of Fluorspar Ore From Mexico
subfiles.from: Pierre de L. Boal, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Reports a proposed Japanese contract for monthly shipments of Mexican fluorspar through Acapulco.
subfiles.summary: Despatch: a Mexico City firm contracted to deliver 5,000 tons of fluorspar ore monthly to a Japanese buyer at Acapulco; William Hamer saw the contract, and General Motors refused to sell thirty trucks; NYK reportedly financed it.

subfiles.title: Clinton letter on Philippine ore exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Calls attention to Philippine exports of iron, copper, manganese, and chrome ore to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Clinton cites a report that Philippine Iron Mines shipped 29,383 tons of iron ore to Japan in December, plus chrome and copper, and urges curtailing the trade.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Delmar S. Clinton
subfiles.from: John C. Davis, Office of Philippine Affairs
subfiles.about: Thanks Clinton for reporting Philippine mineral exports and notes that the Department monitors Philippine export figures.
subfiles.summary: Davis acknowledges Clinton's January 23 letter; the Department follows Philippine export statistics but welcomes such information.

subfiles.title: Senator Bone's transmittal of McRae letter
subfiles.about: Forwards McRae's complaint about copper trolley wire allegedly destined for Japan and requests return of the enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Senator Bone sends Hull W. E. McRae's Seattle letter and asks for its return.

subfiles.title: McRae letter on Seattle trolley wire exports
subfiles.about: Alleges that old Seattle trolley wire could evade the scrap ban by being smelted into ingots for Japan.
subfiles.summary: McRae reports old copper trolley wire going to the Tacoma smelter, to be melted into ingots for Japan, and argues this conflicts with democratic solidarity.

subfiles.title: Negotiations of Japanese Interests to Purchase Petroleum in Peru
subfiles.from: J. F. McGurk, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Reports inquiries into alleged Japanese negotiations for Peruvian petroleum and oil-field surveys.
subfiles.summary: Lima despatch: International Petroleum's manager knew of no Sano Bussan representative surveying Peruvian oil, and Peru's ministries denied knowledge of Japanese activity.

subfiles.title: Review of application to export 4.5 million gallons of gasoline to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Division of Controls and Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Reviews a gasoline export application destined for Japanese naval refining and recommends no change in existing policy.
subfiles.summary: Review of an application to export 4.5 million gallons of gasoline to Japan: not refusable under directives, though for the Japanese Navy and refinable above 87 octane; no new circumstance justified changing policy.

subfiles.title: Editorial survey on American Pacific policy
subfiles.about: Begins reporting a statistical analysis of 939 newspaper editorials on American policy in the Pacific.
subfiles.summary: Price says the committee reviewed editorials from 233 newspapers in 38 states, September 12-October 26, 1940; the page begins a breakdown of attitudes toward aid to China.
